study_identification.title: Individual differences v. the average patient: mapping the heterogeneity in ADHD using normative models

study_characteristics.study_objective: To map biological heterogeneity of persistent ADHD at the individual level using normative modeling, quantifying inter-individual differences in brain structure in reference to normative brain aging across the adult lifespan, and to examine the degree to which case-control analyses disguise differences between individuals.

dataset_name.answer: Dutch cohort of the International Multicenter persistent ADHD CollaboraTion (IMpACT)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: SPM-12 (rigid alignment, segmentation, normalization, bias field correction using 'new segment'); DARTEL (study-specific gray matter template creation); 8-mm FWHM Gaussian kernel smoothing

software_tool.answer: Not explicitly stated (custom implementation based on Gaussian process regression framework)

response_variable.answer: Gray matter volume (voxel-wise); White matter volume (voxel-wise)

predictor_effects.answer: Age and Sex modeled as fixed effects. Sex modeled separately (separate models for females and males).

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study uses Gaussian Process Regression which provides uncertainty estimates, allowing for heteroscedasticity modeling to some extent. The study models males and females separately, suggesting awareness of sex-related variance differences. However, the paper does not explicitly discuss or evaluate how well the model handles various nuisance structures such as within-group variance heterogeneity, potential age-related variance changes, or other sources of nuisance variation. The uncertainty quantification in GPR provides some capability to handle variance structure, but systematic evaluation is not reported.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Gaussian process regression (Rasmussen and Williams, 2006), a Bayesian non-parametric interpolation method that yields coherent measures of predictive confidence in addition to point estimates. This is important, as we used this uncertainty measure to quantify both the centiles of variation within the cohort and the deviation of each patient from the group mean at each specific brain locus. In this way, we were able to statistically quantify deviations from the normative model with regional specificity, by computing a Z-score for each voxel, reflecting the difference between the predicted volume and the true volume normalized by the uncertainty of the prediction.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study explicitly uses 10-fold cross-validation on the healthy control sample to estimate the normative range. This is a same-domain non-independent validation strategy where the training dataset is used for validation through cross-validation, ensuring that predictions are made on held-out portions of the same cohort.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: The normative range for this model in healthy individuals was estimated using 10-fold crossvalidation, then we applied the model trained on all healthy individuals to participants with ADHD. We implemented this framework using 10-fold cross-validation for healthy individuals and out-of-sample validation for individuals with ADHD.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The paper explicitly states that they could not split the healthy control sample into independent training and test sets due to sample size limitations. They used 10-fold cross-validation instead, which is a non-independent validation approach. There was no independent held-out healthy control dataset used for validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: We could not follow the same procedure for controls and cases, due to the size of our sample, as discussed in the limitations paragraph. First, we had to use 10-fold cross-validation in healthy individuals and out of sample predictions in individuals with persistent ADHD, as our healthy sample was too small to split it into two. This potentially introduces a small bias.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Supplemental Methods line 11-12; Main text lines 164-165

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study applies the normative model trained on healthy controls to individuals with ADHD, which represents a different clinical domain. This is an out-of-sample validation on a clinically different population (ADHD patients vs. healthy controls), demonstrating the model's ability to characterize deviations in a different domain.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: The normative range for this model in healthy individuals was estimated using 10-fold crossvalidation, then we applied the model trained on all healthy individuals to participants with ADHD. We implemented this framework using 10-fold cross-validation for healthy individuals and out-of-sample validation for individuals with ADHD.

clinical_dataset.answer: Dutch cohort of the International Multicenter persistent ADHD CollaboraTion (IMpACT)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (threshold |Z| > 2.6 for extreme deviations); percentage of extreme positive deviations; percentage of extreme negative deviations; voxel-wise overlap maps

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group-level deviations analyzed using PALM (Permutation Analysis of Linear Models) with FDR correction at 5%; Wald χ² test for percentage of extreme deviations (with Bonferroni-Holm correction); voxel-wise overlap analysis; Pearson correlations between percentage of extreme deviations and age, symptom scores (hyperactivity/impulsivity, inattention), comorbidity, and stimulant medication (with Bonferroni-Holm correction); Individual-level thresholding at |Z| > 2.6; also repeated with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at individual level.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: While participants with ADHD showed mean deviations in cerebellum, temporal regions, and hippocampus, individual-level extreme deviations showed substantial heterogeneity with only a few brain loci showing extreme negative deviations in more than 2% of ADHD participants, demonstrating that the 'average ADHD patient' concept has limited informative value.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: At the group level, participants with ADHD showed significantly reduced gray matter in cerebellum, temporal regions, and hippocampus compared to healthy individuals (FDR-corrected at 5%). The percentage of extreme negative deviations in gray matter was significantly higher in ADHD (0.48%, 95% CI: 0.30-0.66%) than in healthy controls (0.28%, 95% CI: 0.24-0.34%; Wald χ²(1)=23.64, p<0.001). Similarly, white matter showed significantly higher extreme negative deviations in ADHD (0.41%, 95% CI: 0.24-0.57%) compared to controls (0.24%, 95% CI: 0.17-0.31%; Wald χ²(1)=18.02, p<0.001). However, at the individual level, overlap in extreme negative deviations exceeding 2% was observed only in limited regions (primarily cerebellum, hippocampus, and basal ganglia). Nine out of ten most negatively deviating patients showed extreme values in cerebellum, but in non-overlapping areas. Individual deviation patterns were largely unique for each ADHD participant. In white matter, extreme negative deviations were associated with age in ADHD participants (β=0.198, p=0.014) but not with symptom scores, stimulant medication, or comorbidity before multiple comparison correction. These findings demonstrate substantial biological heterogeneity at the individual level, challenging the concept of the 'average ADHD patient'.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: 1) Small healthy control sample size necessitated 10-fold cross-validation rather than independent train-test split, potentially introducing small bias; 2) No associations found between symptom scores and normative deviations, possibly due to reliance on noisy self-report measures rather than diagnostic interviews; 3) Sample did not allow inspection of comorbidity effects due to inconsistent comorbidities across individuals; 4) Larger studies show reduced predictive accuracy potentially due to capturing more biological and procedural heterogeneity (e.g., scanner differences), though this study used single-site data; 5) Future studies should build population-based normative models on large samples and apply them to cohorts with consistent inclusion criteria.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The authors challenge the traditional case-control paradigm, arguing that it disguises inter-individual differences. They suggest this heterogeneity may explain why case-control studies show small group differences and why pattern classification studies show variable accuracy (60-90% in ADHD, with ADHD-200 competition not exceeding 60%). Unlike voxel-based morphometry and pattern classification approaches that assume group homogeneity, normative modeling allows investigation of individual differences without this assumption. The study provides the first quantitative estimate of biological heterogeneity in ADHD in terms of spatial overlap of individual extreme deviations. Authors emphasize need to move toward individual-level descriptions of biology to improve understanding and nosology of ADHD, and suggest that larger, more representative samples capture more heterogeneity, making it harder to find common decision functions in classification analyses.
